reply.question: What is Inner Monologue, and how does it give streaming ASR and TTS?
reply.text:
No written answer this time: here are the most relevant passages from the papers, quoted as they are.
[S1] 2410.00037v1 p.31 §5.7: "Metrics. Section 3.4.4 and Appendix C describe how Inner Monologue can provide a streaming TTS or streaming ASR system by simply changing the delay it uses between text and audio tokens. In particular, we train a streaming TTS model by delaying audio tokens by 2 seconds, giving some lookahead to the text tokens, and teacher forcing text tokens at inference. Similarly, we train a streaming ASR model by delaying text tokens by 2 seconds, allowing the model to listen to audio content before generating text tokens. In that case, at inference we teacher force the audio tokens."
[S2] 2410.00037v1 pp.41-42 §7: "To summarize, we introduce a complete suite of models and recipes, from text LLMs to neural audio codecs and generative audio models, which we combine into a real-time spoken dialogue system with a 160ms theoretical latency able to follow complex multi-turn conversations across 5 minutes. We release both Mimi and Moshi to foster the development of such applications. Additionally, we show how our Inner Monologue method allows designing streaming TTS and streaming ASR just by changing the delay between text and audio tokens."
[S3] 2410.00037v1 p.5 §2: "Moreover, Inner Monologue decomposes speech on a per-frame basis, which means that each prediction step outputs a speech frame. This is unlike Spectron which requires generating a complete sequence as text before generating audio tokens, and this makes Moshi compatible with real-time generation. Finally, we show in Section 3.4.4 how Inner Monologue, when combined with a delay between token types, allows deriving streaming TTS and ASR systems from Moshi. Spoken Dialogue Models."

reply.question: In simple terms, what does scaled dot-product attention compute, and why divide the query-key dot products by sqrt(d_k)?
reply.text:
Scaled‑dot‑product attention takes a query vector and a set of key–value pairs, computes the compatibility of the query with each key by a dot product, and then uses those scores to form a weighted sum of the corresponding values [S3].  
All dot products are first divided by √dₖ, where dₖ is the dimension of the queries and keys [S1].  
This scaling prevents the raw dot products from becoming excessively large when dₖ is big, which would push the subsequent soft‑max into regions with very small gradients [S1].  
By keeping the magnitude of the scores moderate, the soft‑max yields more stable attention weights and better learning dynamics [S1].

reply.question: How are the positional encodings built, and why sinusoids rather than learned embeddings?
reply.text:
The Transformer adds a positional encoding vector to each token embedding, where the encoding has the same dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) and is defined by sine and cosine functions of varying frequencies: for even indices \(2i\) it uses \(\sin(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\) and for odd indices \(2i+1\) it uses \(\cos(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\) so that each dimension corresponds to a sinusoid whose wavelength forms a geometric progression [S1].  
These sinusoidal encodings were chosen because a fixed offset \(k\) between positions can be expressed as a linear function of the original encodings, making it easy for the model to learn relative positions [S1].  
The authors also tried learned positional embeddings and found that performance was nearly the same as with sinusoids [S2].  
However, they preferred the sinusoidal version because it can generalize to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, whereas learned embeddings are limited to the lengths they were trained on [S1][S2].

reply.question: Per Table 1, how does self-attention compare with recurrent layers on complexity per layer, sequential operations and maximum path length?
reply.text:
Self‑attention layers have a per‑layer computational complexity of \(O(n^{2}\,d)\), require only a constant number of sequential operations \(O(1)\), and have a maximum path length of \(O(1)\) between any two positions [S2].  
Recurrent layers, in contrast, cost \(O(n\,d^{2})\) per layer, need \(O(n)\) sequential operations, and their maximum path length also scales as \(O(n)\) [S2].  
Thus, self‑attention is computationally more expensive than recurrent layers only when the sequence length \(n\) exceeds the representation dimension \(d\), but it offers far greater parallelism (constant‑time sequential depth) and a dramatically shorter longest dependency path [S1][S2].

No written answer this time: here are the most relevant passages from the papers, quoted as they are.
[S1] 2507.07955v2 p.22 §4: "Deeper Hierarchies. H-Net is the first dynamic hierarchical model that can recursively nest its chunking strategy (see Table 6 and Appendix A). In this paper, we showed that iterating H-Net from 0 stages (i.e. an isotropic model) to 1 stage and from 1 stage to 2 stages consistently improves performance. We did not attempt a 3-stage H-Net at all for simplicity. Testing if H-Net can be iterated even deeper remains an immediate direction to explore. Global Sequence Model Considerations."
[S2] 2410.00037v1 p.2 §1: "Voice has provided a convenient interface to early conversational systems, from Alexa^1 to Siri^2 and Google Assistant.^3 In this context, a “wake word” spoken by the user typically triggers an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system which transcribes the subsequent user’s request. Then, a natural language understanding (NLU) pipeline converts this query to a structured format used to produce a text answer through natural language generation (NLG). [S3] 2507.07955v2 p.32 §A.1.3 (appendix): "2025) is a concurrent work that augments SpaceByte with additional stages of hierarchy using fixed-width chunking. Specifically, AU-Net 2 is SpaceByte with minor architectural modifications, while AU-Net 3 (and AU-Net 4) add additional levels of hierarchical with width-2 downsampling. In this work, we show that SpaceByte’s delimiter chunking strategy can be a very powerful baseline on appropriate languages – competitive with or outperforming traditional tokenizers on English and code – when augmented with several of H-Net’s additional techniques (Section 3.1, Section 3.3, Figure 5, Figure 9)."
